routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more reasonable than skeptical atheism through convergent cosmological, design, moral, historical, and experiential evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the principal evidence is substantially more expected under a transcendent personal and morally good creator revealed through Jesus than under skeptical atheism, while answering the strongest naturalistic alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative evidence makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent personal cause.
Life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than necessity or chance.
Objective moral values and duties exist and are best grounded in a morally perfect God.
The resurrection evidence and immediate experience support the specifically Christian identification of God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: An actually infinite temporal regress is metaphysically impossible.
The empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief are historical facts best explained by resurrection.

routes.description: Defeat the comparative case for Christian theism by exposing underdetermination, unreliable methods, natural alternatives, and contrary moral evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that Craig's evidence does not reliably discriminate the Christian God from natural, unknown, or rival supernatural explanations and that the observed world supplies significant contrary evidence.

motionBridge.description: The presented evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Religious belief and experience are culturally variable and psychologically unreliable without independent corroboration.
Current cosmology and ordinary causal experience do not warrant an absolute beginning or an immaterial personal cause.
Fine-tuning and morality fail to discriminate the Christian God from naturalistic or rival supernatural explanations.
Weak and dependent resurrection sources plus the world's evil undermine the specifically Christian perfect-God hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Observed intelligence depends on physical structures, weakening inference to a disembodied mind.
Rapidly changing frontier physics warrants caution about conclusions concerning ultimate origins.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning, causation, and a personal cause
sections.rationale: The Kalam exchange is the debate's most sustained contested route, covering actual infinity, the BGV theorem, causation from nothing, composition, and the inference to mind.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The universe began to exist, whatever begins to exist has a cause, and the resulting transcendent cause is best identified as an unembodied personal mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there must have been a transcendent cause which brought the universe into being

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span falls unambiguously within Craig's uninterrupted opening presentation and uses his announced first argument.

response.rationale: This is Craig's first constructive statement and has no earlier selected argumentative target requiring a response.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is explicit, but the movement among local universe, global universe, spacetime boundary, and absolute beginning compresses material scope distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is presented as necessary although the scientific premise and the exhaustive abstract-object-or-mind inference retain substantial disputed assumptions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The formal core is valid, but the transition from a first cause to a timeless personal mind relies on substantial implicit exhaustiveness and agency bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig supplies philosophical examples and a named cosmological theorem, yet the theorem's scope and the extrapolation from beginnings within nature remain materially contestable.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly develops the announced cosmological route, though it necessarily answers no selected earlier move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The argument materially advances the declared central cosmology bridge by supplying both a beginning premise and a proposed personal cause.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not depend on a developed representation of a live selected opponent alternative, so charity is not tested.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Craig explicitly presents the infinite-past argument, the BGV theorem, the causal syllogism, and the abstract-object versus mind inference in this span.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Neither causal experience nor current cosmology warrants Craig's absolute beginning and personal-cause conclusion; the causal premise is extrapolated beyond its evidence and the BGV theorem permits relevant qualifications.

sourceSpan.excerpt: all we know here is that our science cannot cope with it trying to draw any firm conclusion seems wishful thinking

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is within Millican's uninterrupted opening case and explicitly identifies and criticizes Craig's Kalam premises.

components.text: The universal causal premise applies to creation ex nihilo and to the universe as a whole.
The evidence establishes an absolute beginning of the complete physical universe.
A nonphysical cause must be an unembodied personal mind rather than an unknown kind of cause.

response.rationale: Millican directly contests every indispensable stage: causal extrapolation, global beginning, and identification of the cause as a disembodied mind.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican explicitly distinguishes local from global universe and separates causal, temporal, and personal-cause objections.

calibrationFindings.rationale: His skepticism is repeatedly qualified, although language such as completely unpersuasive is somewhat stronger than the underdetermination established.

charity.alternative: Craig's strongest case combines a metaphysical causal principle with philosophical and BGV-based arguments for an absolute beginning.
charity.decisiveQualification: The BGV result concerns average expansion and does not by itself exhaust contracting or unknown global cosmologies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objections are clearly separated and jointly support underdetermination without requiring Millican to prove an eternal universe.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: He gives specific theorem qualifications, cosmological alternatives, and limits of causal experience, with some dependence on broad claims about frontier physics.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts all three indispensable components of Craig's Kalam route and focuses on their inferential sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the declared central cosmology bridge rather than merely discussing peripheral cosmological possibilities.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican reconstructs the syllogism as valid and targets its premises and personal-cause extension, while preserving Craig's actual route.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The selected span contains the causal-experience objection, local/global distinction, BGV qualification, quantum-gravity caution, and mind-body objection.

sections.title: Fine-tuning, design, and competing explanations
sections.rationale: Both speakers treat fine-tuning as genuinely explanatory evidence while contesting probability, future physics, multiverses, divine efficiency, and its ability to identify the Christian God.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The narrow life-permitting range of constants and initial conditions is not plausibly due to necessity or chance and therefore supports a cosmic designer.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the fine-tuning is not due to either physical necessity or chance from which we may conclude therefore it is due to design

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's explicitly numbered second opening argument and remains within his uninterrupted speech.

response.rationale: This move opens the selected fine-tuning issue and has no earlier selected opponent move to answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-way explanatory structure is clear, but the relevant probability space and scope of physical necessity are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inference treats necessity, chance, and design as exhaustive and chance as eliminated without adequately qualifying the uncertain possibility distribution.

charity.alternative: Chance or a deeper physical explanation could account for apparently life-permitting constants without intentional design.
charity.decisiveQualification: The force of chance depends on a justified probability distribution over genuinely possible universes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive route is intelligible, but the exhaustiveness of the trilemma and the move from improbability plus pattern to design remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument cites constants and initial conditions but supplies no detailed probability measure or representative quantitative case within the selected span.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it efficiently states and develops the fine-tuning case without an earlier selected response obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the declared central fine-tuning bridge and supplies its principal explanatory comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The chance alternative is recognizable, but it is compressed into random selection without fully presenting selection effects or deeper-law possibilities.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Craig identifies constants and initial conditions, describes a narrow life-permitting range, and argues by eliminating physical necessity and chance.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Fine-tuning is intriguing but presently underdetermined because probability claims are based on one universe, deeper physics or multiverses remain possible, and the observed cosmos poorly discriminates a perfect Christian God from an evil or limited designer.

sourceSpan.excerpt: this constitutes a phenomenon which very naturally invites explanation in terms of a cosmic scale designer but I also see good reason for caution and modesty here

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's expressly announced fine-tuning rebuttal in an uninterrupted turn with consistent first-person framing.

components.text: The constants occupy an independently warranted, extremely improbable life-permitting range.
Physical necessity or a deeper future theory is not a viable explanation.
Chance, including multiverse selection effects, is less plausible than design.
The design inference specifically favors an omniscient, omnipotent, morally perfect Christian God.

response.rationale: Millican answers the probabilistic and rival-explanation core but partly shifts from Craig's limited designer conclusion to the fuller Christian hypothesis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concessions, uncertainty claims, alternative explanations, and discrimination objection are clearly separated and repeatedly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Millican expressly treats design as a natural possible explanation while limiting his conclusion to present caution and underdetermination.

charity.alternative: Craig's strongest fine-tuning claim is an abductive inference to a powerful designer, not by itself a complete proof of moral perfection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig assigns the designer's goodness to a separate moral argument, so anti-God does not directly refute the limited design conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The several cautions coherently establish underdetermination, though some objections address Christian specification rather than the limited design inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply offers concrete alternatives and observational proportions, but some numerical illustrations and future-physics expectations are asserted rather than documented.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts most decisive fine-tuning components but does not fully answer Craig's narrower claim that design alone is favored over necessity and chance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central fine-tuning bridge through probability, selection-effect, and rival-designer objections.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican grants the argument's genuine pull and states a strong conditional version, while occasionally evaluating it against more than Craig claimed it alone proved.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Millican concedes the apparent coincidence, then develops sample-size, future-law, multiverse, anti-God, inefficiency, scale, and extraterrestrial objections.

sections.title: Objective morality, naturalism, and evil
sections.rationale: The moral argument is contested at both ontological and evidential levels, with disagreement about intrinsic value, obligation, moral realism, and whether evil instead counts against a perfect God.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, would not exist without God, and therefore support the existence and goodness of God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if God did not exist objective moral values and duties would not exist

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's explicitly numbered third opening argument and is clearly attributable throughout.

response.rationale: The move constructively introduces both premises and the conclusion of the moral argument without an earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Craig defines objective as belief-independent, but shifts among values, duties, bindingness, and grounding without fully distinguishing their ontologies.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is called logically inescapable although the crucial no-God conditional rests largely on selected testimony and naturalistic genealogy.

charity.alternative: Naturalists may accept stance-independent moral truths or construct binding standards from rationality, welfare, or sentiment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explaining the causal origin of moral belief does not itself show that all nontheistic moral standards are illusory.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modus-tollens structure is clear, but the grounding premise does not follow merely from evolutionary influence on moral cognition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral experience and quotations support the existence premise more than the contested claim that only a divine source can ground value and obligation.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly states the moral route, though it does not yet engage a selected opponent formulation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral bridge by attempting to establish both objective morality and its divine ground.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats naturalistic moral belief mainly as adaptive herd conditioning and omits stronger nontheistic realist accounts relevant to its conclusion.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Craig defines belief-independent value, invokes evolutionary accounts, appeals to moral apprehension, and concludes that God grounds objective good and evil.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Nontheists can be moral realists and recognize intrinsic human value, so Craig has not explained why objective moral truth or its apprehension depends ontologically on God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are plenty of moral realists who are not theists and I don't understand why Bill wants to say that as an atheist one must presuppose that humans have no intrinsic value

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is Millican's final rebuttal, where he explicitly returns to and sharpens his challenge to Craig's moral argument.

components.text: Objective moral values and duties are genuinely apprehended as belief-independent.
Objective moral values and duties require God as their ontological ground.
Binding moral obligations specifically require a personal divine prescriber.

response.rationale: Millican directly challenges divine grounding and human-value claims but does not fully engage Craig's distinct prescriber account of obligation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding challenge is clear, although Millican continues to flag rather than resolve the multiple senses of objective morality.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He presents the position as a challenge and openly concedes difficulty in fully spelling out why some values are intrinsically valuable.

charity.alternative: Craig distinguishes knowing moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objective and binding.
charity.decisiveQualification: The mere existence of atheist moral realists does not itself establish that their proposed grounding is adequate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemic-versus-ontological distinction is recognized and the challenge exposes an explanatory gap, though survey prevalence is not a grounding argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The survey and examples establish that nontheistic realism is a live position, but they provide limited affirmative support for any particular ontology.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts the main divine-grounding premise but leaves the separate moral-obligation and prescriber inference substantially unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central moral bridge by disputing the claimed dependence of objective value on God.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican accurately identifies Craig's ontological rather than merely epistemic claim and targets that stronger formulation.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The span cites the philosopher survey, distinguishes moral knowledge from ontology, and argues that rational and valuable human characteristics remain available to atheists.

sections.title: Resurrection evidence and historical inference
sections.rationale: The specifically Christian step depends heavily on the historical status and explanatory force of the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and sudden origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are widely accepted facts best explained by God's raising Jesus from the dead.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are actually three facts recognized by the majority of historians today which I believe are best explained by the resurrection of Jesus

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's explicitly numbered fourth opening argument and consistently presents his historical case.

response.rationale: This selected move opens the resurrection issue and therefore has no earlier selected target or response components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three alleged facts and resurrection conclusion are readily recoverable, though majority and plausible naturalistic explanation remain loosely quantified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig moves from contested historical claims to no plausible naturalistic explanation without discussing source dependence, legendary development, or prior probability.

charity.alternative: Natural explanations include legendary growth, grief experiences, cognitive dissonance, mistaken reports, or combinations of these mechanisms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting older theft or apparent-death theories does not exhaust the naturalistic explanatory space.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Inference to the best explanation is coherent, but its force depends on an underdeveloped comparison set and an implicit bridge from resurrection to divine authorization.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig names scholars and three data points, but gives little source-critical argument for independence, reliability, or superiority over broader natural explanations.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly advances the historical route without an earlier selected response burden.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the declared subsidiary resurrection-facts bridge, a necessary component of the specifically Christian route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Natural alternatives are represented mainly by two older theories and then treated as exhausted, omitting stronger psychological and transmission accounts.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Craig identifies the empty tomb, appearances, and transformed disciple belief, cites scholarly acceptance, and claims resurrection best explains them.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: The Gospel reports are late, partisan, textually dependent, discrepant, and weakly corroborated, so they are insufficient evidence for overturning the ordinary naturalistic understanding of death.

sourceSpan.excerpt: these are not independent reports but even so they contain many discrepancies

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's explicitly introduced treatment of resurrection evidence in his final rebuttal.

components.text: The empty tomb is a sufficiently secure and independently attested historical fact.
Different individuals and groups experienced appearances requiring a risen Jesus explanation.
The disciples' resurrection belief arose despite predispositions and lacks a plausible natural explanation.
A bodily resurrection is the best overall explanation of all three facts.

response.rationale: Millican directly attacks source quality and the miracle inference but does not fully analyze the origin and persistence of the earliest disciples' belief in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical objections are concrete and scoped to the evidential adequacy of the Gospel reports.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence warrants substantial caution, though describing the case as feeble somewhat outruns the brief source analysis supplied.

charity.alternative: Craig's case rests on three purportedly multiply attested historical facts rather than on accepting every Gospel detail as accurate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Discrepancies in peripheral passion details do not by themselves disprove the three claimed core facts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence, authorship, discrepancy, and corroboration points coherently reduce evidential force, though some cited anomalies are peripheral to the core facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Millican gives specific source relationships and examples, but relies on compressed scholarly assertions and does not compare detailed explanatory likelihoods.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts source reliability and the best-explanation claim but incompletely addresses the disciples' original belief component.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the declared subsidiary bridge concerning the historical status and explanation of the resurrection facts.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican recognizes the historical-evidence form of the argument, although his emphasis on spectacular Matthean details is not central to Craig's three-fact case.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Millican cites late non-eyewitness authorship, Markan and Q dependence, Gospel discrepancies, canonical selection, and missing external corroboration.

sections.title: Religious experience, disagreement, and evidential burden
sections.rationale: The debate's cumulative comparison turns on whether immediate religious experience is a legitimate independent source and whether widespread conflicting religions defeat its reliability.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: A sincere seeker can know God immediately through personal experience apart from argument, and the cumulative evidence leaves atheism without a comparably supported case.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if you're sincerely seeking God God will make his existence evident to you

proMoves.attributionBasis: The argumentative portion begins in Craig's uninterrupted opening conclusion before the moderator transition within the recorded span.

response.rationale: This is the initial selected statement of Craig's experiential route and therefore carries no earlier selected response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Immediate experience and sincere seeking are understandable, but evidential, salvific, and psychological senses of making God evident are not distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The promise that sincere seeking will make God evident is asserted categorically without a public reliability test or treatment of sincere nonbelief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experiential claim can function as first-person justification, but its extension to a general comparative conclusion lacks an articulated reliability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on scriptural promise and phenomenological assertion rather than independent evidence capable of discriminating competing religious experiences.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it advances Craig's fifth consideration, although the selected span also compresses the broader burden claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central Christian-evidence bridge by claiming immediate experiential access to the identified God.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed live opponent alternative is represented in this constructive, so the charity test is not activated.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Craig distinguishes experience from argument, invokes immediate awareness and sincere seeking, and folds it into his cumulative conclusion.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Religious experience is unreliable because similar culturally transmitted methods generate many incompatible beliefs, and its claims require psychological and independent evidential testing.

sourceSpan.excerpt: religious experience is an extremely unreliable method of knowledge or alleged knowledge people have religious experiences of all sorts

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's closing speech, explicitly responding to Craig's claim that religious experience went unanswered.

components.text: Immediate religious experience can provide knowledge of the specifically Christian God.
Sincere seeking reliably results in God making his existence evident.
The experiential route helps make Christian theism comparatively better supported than skeptical atheism.

response.rationale: Millican directly challenges experiential reliability, offers conflicting experiences as a defeater, and identifies experimental psychology as the appropriate replacement test.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection clearly concerns reliability rather than a genetic inference from origins directly to falsity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Conflicting traditions strongly support caution, though the blanket description extremely unreliable exceeds the limited empirical detail supplied here.

charity.alternative: Craig presents personal experience as immediate warrant supplemented by public logic and evidence, not as the sole shared method of all religions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conflicting experiences undermine reliability unless Craig supplies a discriminator; they do not deductively prove every experience false.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move avoids the genetic fallacy and instead draws a reliability consequence from similar methods producing incompatible outputs.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cross-religious conflict and natural psychological mechanisms are pertinent evidence, though the promised experimental account remains mostly programmatic.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts every indispensable experiential component and directly explains why the proposed method does not discriminate Christianity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central Christian-evidence bridge by challenging the reliability and comparative force of religious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican accurately treats the experience claim as alleged knowledge and targets its reliability while allowing that further empirical testing is needed.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Millican invokes diverse experiences, natural psychological mechanisms, multiple fantastic traditions, and the need for experimental rather than merely textual assessment.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains outside the selected ratings, response links, importance judgments, section weights, or omission treatment.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No independent completion criterion is altered beyond the route and move judgments already recorded.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No distinct unscored debate-wide consequence was identified for the pro side.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing any alleged residual consequence would not change the pro route's completion status independently of the scored ledger.

con.rationale: The late problem-of-evil material and other omissions are already reflected in route framing, selected exchanges, weights, and move-level judgments.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No independent completion criterion is altered beyond the route and move judgments already recorded.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No distinct unscored debate-wide consequence was identified for the con side.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing any alleged residual consequence would not change the con route's completion status independently of the scored ledger.
